questions.question: Inguinal hernias in children are almost always caused by:

options.A: A direct defect in the abdominal wall muscles

questions.explanation: Inguinal hernias in children are almost always indirect, caused by failure of the processus vaginalis (the tongue of peritoneum that precedes testicular descent) to obliterate after birth.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Inguinal Hernias

questions.question: A patent processus vaginalis that allows peritoneal fluid (but no bowel) to track down into the scrotum results in:
questions.explanation: When a patent processus vaginalis allows only peritoneal fluid (not bowel) to track into the scrotum, the result is a hydrocoele — typically a non-tender, transilluminating scrotal swelling, distinct from an inguinal hernia where bowel or other abdominal content is present.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery

questions.question: A 'retractile' testis is distinguished from a true undescended testis by the fact that:

options.A: A retractile testis can be manipulated without tension into the base of the scrotum, though it is pulled back up by the cremaster muscle
options.B: A retractile testis is always impalpable
options.C: A retractile testis requires orchidopexy immediately
options.D: There is no meaningful difference between the two

questions.explanation: A retractile testis can be brought down to the base of the scrotum without tension, but is then pulled back up by an overactive cremaster reflex — over time it usually resides permanently in the scrotum, though follow-up is still advised as it can rarely re-ascend and require orchidopexy.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Undescended Testes

questions.question: Orchidopexy for a palpable undescended testis is ideally performed at what age, to optimise fertility outcomes?

options.D: Age has no bearing on fertility outcomes

questions.explanation: Orchidopexy is ideally performed as a day-case procedure between 6 and 12 months of age. Bringing the testis into the scrotum (below core body temperature) at a young age optimises spermatogenesis and fertility outcomes.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Undescended Testes

questions.question: In a child presenting with acute scrotal pain, testicular torsion must be relieved within approximately what time window from symptom onset for a good chance of testicular salvage?
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion must be relieved within 6-8 hours of symptom onset for a good chance of salvaging the testis — this is why any acute scrotum where torsion cannot be confidently excluded requires urgent surgical exploration.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — The Acute Scrotum

questions.question: The 'blue dot sign' on the scrotum in a boy just before puberty is classically associated with:

options.B: Torsion of a testicular/epididymal appendage (hydatid of Morgagni)

questions.explanation: Torsion of a testicular or epididymal appendage (hydatid of Morgagni) characteristically affects boys just before puberty, and the torted, infarcted appendage may occasionally be visible or palpable through the scrotal skin as a tender bluish nodule — the 'blue dot sign'.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — The Acute Scrotum

questions.question: In hypospadias, why is ritual/routine circumcision specifically contraindicated in the newborn period?

options.A: Circumcision is never contraindicated in any condition
options.B: The foreskin is often needed later for the surgical reconstruction of the hypospadias
options.D: It has no bearing on hypospadias management at all

questions.explanation: In hypospadias, the deficient ventral foreskin tissue is often required for the surgical reconstruction of the urethra later on, so removing it via routine circumcision in infancy would compromise the corrective surgery.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery

questions.question: True phimosis, as distinguished from a normal non-retractile foreskin in a young boy, is characterised by:

options.A: Simple inability to retract the foreskin at age 2, which is entirely normal
options.B: Whitish scarring of the foreskin caused by balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO), rarely seen before age 5
options.C: Ballooning of the foreskin during urination with no scarring
options.D: A condition that always requires surgery in infancy

questions.explanation: 'Phimosis' is often wrongly applied to a normal non-retractile foreskin, which is common and physiological in young boys. True phimosis is pathological whitish scarring caused by balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO), and is rare before 5 years of age.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — The Foreskin and Circumcision

questions.question: An umbilical hernia in an infant, caused by incomplete closure of the umbilical ring, most commonly:

options.B: Resolves spontaneously by around 4 years of age
options.C: Always requires surgical repair within the first month of life
options.D: Is a surgical emergency due to a very high incarceration rate

questions.explanation: Umbilical hernias are common in infants and most resolve spontaneously by around 4 years of age, with incarceration being very rare — unlike supraumbilical hernias, which do not close on their own and are repaired around the same age.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Midline Hernias

questions.question: A child injured by a bicycle handlebar to the abdomen is classically at risk of injury to which structures?

options.B: Pancreatic, duodenal, mesenteric, or liver trauma
options.C: The small intestine or lumbar spine only
options.D: Severe crush injury to the chest exclusively

questions.explanation: Handlebar injuries classically cause focal, high-pressure blunt trauma to the upper abdomen, putting the pancreas, duodenum, mesentery, or liver at risk — distinct from lap belt injuries (small intestine/lumbar spine) or straddle injuries (urethra/pelvis).
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Paediatric Trauma, Patterns of Injury

questions.question: Isolated blunt liver or splenic injury in a haemodynamically stable child is generally best managed by:
questions.explanation: Isolated liver or splenic injury in a stable child can usually be managed non-operatively, with laparotomy reserved for ongoing intra-abdominal bleeding; uncomplicated cases can often be discharged after 5-7 days with a period of restricted activity.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Paediatric Trauma

questions.question: The final descent of the testis into the scrotum during fetal development is mediated primarily by:

options.C: Growth hormone from the fetal pituitary

questions.explanation: While gonadal induction (forming a testis in the first place) is driven by genes on the Y chromosome and initial abdominal migration is guided by the gubernaculum, the final descent of the testis into the scrotum is mediated by testosterone produced by the fetal testis itself.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Genital Development

questions.question: In prolonged fasting (beyond 48-72 hours), the central nervous system adapts to using which fuel source as primary, reducing the need for muscle protein breakdown?
questions.explanation: After 48-72 hours of fasting, the CNS adapts to using ketone bodies (produced by hepatic ketogenesis from fatty acids, facilitated by low insulin) as its primary fuel source — this 'fat fuel economy' shift reduces the need for muscle breakdown by up to 55 g per day compared to simple short-term starvation.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutrition and Fluid Therapy — Metabolic Response to Starvation

questions.question: How does the metabolic response to trauma/sepsis differ from simple starvation regarding ketone formation?

options.A: Both produce identical, unimpaired ketone formation
options.B: In trauma/sepsis, ketone formation is impaired, and glucose-generating protein breakdown cannot be entirely prevented even by giving glucose
options.C: Trauma always increases ketone formation far beyond that seen in starvation
options.D: Ketone formation is irrelevant to both conditions

questions.explanation: Unlike simple starvation (where glucose administration can readily reverse protein catabolism), trauma and sepsis patients have impaired ketone formation, and gluconeogenesis (protein breakdown to make glucose) cannot be entirely prevented by giving exogenous glucose — a key nutritional distinction between the two states.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutrition and Fluid Therapy — Metabolic Response to Trauma and Sepsis

questions.question: Why is serum albumin considered an unreliable direct measure of a patient's nutritional status, especially in the acute setting?

options.A: Albumin levels never change regardless of nutrition or illness
options.B: Hypoalbuminaemia often results from altered body fluid composition and increased capillary permeability related to sepsis, not nutrition alone
options.C: Albumin can only be measured once per year
options.D: Albumin is only produced by the kidneys, unrelated to nutrition

questions.explanation: Although a low serum albumin (<30 g/L) is a poor prognostic indicator, hypoalbuminaemia is frequently driven by alterations in body fluid composition and increased capillary permeability from ongoing sepsis or illness — not purely by nutritional intake — so albumin is not a reliable direct marker of nutritional status, particularly acutely.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery

questions.question: A BMI below which threshold is associated with significant hospital mortality risk?
questions.explanation: A BMI of less than 18.5 indicates nutritional impairment, but a BMI below 15 specifically is associated with significant hospital mortality risk.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutritional Assessment — Body Weight and Anthropometry

questions.question: Unintentional weight loss of more than what percentage of body weight over the preceding 6 months is considered a good indicator of poor prognosis?

options.D: Weight loss is never prognostically significant

questions.explanation: Unintentional weight loss of more than 10% of a patient's body weight over the preceding 6 months is considered a good prognostic indicator of poor outcome.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutritional Assessment — Body Weight and Anthropometry

questions.question: What is the minimum daily urine output generally required to adequately excrete the end products of protein metabolism?
questions.explanation: A minimum urine output of approximately 400 mL/day is required to excrete the nitrogenous end products of protein metabolism, even though average daily urine output in a healthy adult is around 1500 mL/day.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery

questions.question: The Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) uses which three components to calculate overall risk of undernutrition?

options.A: BMI, recent weight loss, and the acute disease effect (likely absence of nutritional intake)
options.B: Blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature only

questions.explanation: The MUST tool combines three scored components — BMI, percentage weight loss over 3-6 months, and the acute disease effect (adding points if there has been or will likely be little/no nutritional intake for 5+ days) — to classify overall undernutrition risk as low, medium, or high.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Nutritional Assessment — Clinical, The MUST Tool
